2.0.0.en: 1 Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them to present himself before the LORD. 2 And the LORD said unto Satan, From whence comest thou? And Satan answered the LORD, and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it. 3 And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? and still he holdeth fast his integrity, although thou movedst me against him, to destroy him without cause. 4 And Satan answered the LORD, and said, Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life. 5 But put forth thine hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse thee to thy face. 6 And the LORD said unto Satan, Behold, he is in thine hand; but preserve his soul.

2.0.1.en: “Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them to present himself before the LORD” [1].

2.0.2.en: The enemy came to obtain permission for harsher and more bitter temptations, for the dragon “accuseth them before our God day and night” (Rev 12:10).

2.0.3.en: * “Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD” [1]. Why does the writer present the idea of their coming in this way every day?

2.0.4.en: So that we may realize that the event itself does not escape divine providence, and that the angels give an account of the events of every day, and that every day they are sent to settle matters, even when we fail to realize this; for they were created for this. This is their work, as Paul says: “(Are they not all) ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?” (Heb 1:14)...

2.0.5.en: Behold, you see for what purpose the angels were present; but as for him (Satan), what was his purpose? To tempt Job, and to have matters proceed toward the fulfillment of this purpose.

2.0.6.en: Why was he questioned again before the angels? It had to be so, for he had already said before them: [Surely he will blaspheme you to your face] (cf. Job 1:11). What a shame! How did he dare to return and stand among them?

2.1.3.en: From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it” [2].

2.1.4.en: His answer came exactly as the first time, as though he had never harmed anyone at all, and indeed as though it were his right to wrong others. He did not admit that he had sinned!

2.1.5.en: * The aim in his temptations was to direct (Job) toward death, yet by the very same blow he gained growth in his life. Our ancient enemy was grieved that Job's virtues were multiplied by the very means by which he aimed to remove them from him. Although he saw that he had been defeated in the first round, he prepared himself to aim fresh assaults of temptations, and he still had the audacity to speak evil of that saint. For the wicked cannot believe in the existence of the good, even when it is proved by experience...

2.1.6.en: “From whence comest thou?”... (Job 2:2) It is as though the voice of God were saying to him plainly: “Behold, a single man has defeated you; he has defeated you in spite of the weaknesses of the body that he endures, you who struggle to stand before Me, the Creator of all.”

2.1.8.en: * “And Satan answered” (then he answered). This means that when he received authority to speak, when the Lord gave the wicked servant permission to open his mouth before Him, when He commanded that one whose tongue had been held like an immovable pillar. He says: “I have quickly observed the whole earth, and I have set snares in every place, and prepared traps. All places are full of my traps, all have been constrained by my nets, and they were caught in my toil. There is no way of escape from my captivity, for my strategic plans take many forms.

2.1.9.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Note that he goes about the world at every moment. Zechariah teaches us that the angels go to and fro on the earth (Zech 1:10-11). But this wretched one is not content with going about, for divine providence also does this work; rather, he goes about in order to be condemned the more (for his evils), and so that we may be all the more watchful. For this reason he was called [the ruler of the darkness of this age] (Eph 6:12); that is, the ruler of evil.

2.1.10.en: Speak, O Satan, what have you done?

2.1.11.en: He says: I have made a tour of the earth, I have gone around in it, and here I am.

2.1.13.en: He brought nothing useful or good; therefore he did not answer why he made the tour.

2.2.0.en: “And the LORD said unto Satan: Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth?

2.2.1.en: A perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil.

2.2.2.en: And still he holdeth fast his integrity, although thou movedst me against him, to destroy him without cause” [3].

2.2.3.en: Once again the Judge Himself defends the accused and praises him.

2.2.4.en: * Since (God) is just, it was not possible for Him to be moved against him without cause. Again, since He is truth, it was not possible for Him to speak other than in this manner: He was indeed moved against him without cause. But the two go together, in that He is both just and true; He speaks the truth and does no injustice. Let us realize that the blessed Job, for his part, was smitten without cause, and also, in another sense, is not smitten without cause... for he could not have been presented to others as an example of virtue had he not been tried...

2.2.6.en: * Job was not shaken, for he did not retreat from the firmness of his faith.

2.2.7.en: St. Augustine Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job is a type of the person of the Lord Christ, who accepted suffering, “wrath,” without cause; He suffered without cause, and as Savior and intercessor, a propitiation for us, He suffered for a cause, that He might cleanse us by His blood from our sins.

2.2.8.en: * Why does he return to attack? What do we learn from this? Even if we fall a thousand times, Satan will not stop, but continues the war without any hesitation.

2.3.0.en: “And Satan answered the LORD, and said:

2.3.1.en: Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life” [4].

2.3.2.en: This proverb was common in ancient times, in the days of Job, and it expresses valuing a man's life above everything in the world; many interpretations of it have been offered.

2.3.3.en: Perhaps it refers to an ancient custom of bartering the skins of slain animals that hunters pursue. The hungry hunter offers the skins of the animal he has hunted in return for food, and if necessary, when hunger intensifies, he offers all the skins of the animals he has hunted in return for bread to save his life. It is as though this proverb expresses a man's acceptance of the greatest possible losses so as not to lose what is greater, namely his life. The Turkish proverb says: “It is fitting that we offer our beard to save our heads.”

2.3.4.en: Satan wanted to crush Job's character by saying: “Skin for skin,” meaning that whatever he loses, even if it be his children, so long as he is in health, with no one touching his skin, he does not care. He does not care about the lives of his children, but rises up in rage and loses his faith and his sense if anyone touches his skin. He is like the ostrich, which is hard on her young ones as though they were not hers (Job 39:13). He is selfish, a lover of himself, occupied with his health, his comfort and the soundness of his body and nothing else?

2.3.5.en: * What he means by this saying is that the most important thing a man has is himself. All the rest are secondary matters... On this basis I wish to hunt him himself, for wealth is not of great value in the eyes of men.

2.3.6.en: Let us listen, beloved, even if we are ashamed to learn from Satan, that it is fitting for a man to give up everything for his life. And that this is a natural thing for human beings, for no negligence is permitted us when we blaspheme because of wealth. He says that wealth amounts to nothing, so we cast it away entirely for the sake of our life.

2.3.7.en: St. John Chrysostom *Behold the cunning of the adversary, and how violent he was in sin... He knows the difference between outward and inward things. He knows that even the philosophers of this world call the former (outward) things adiafora, of no value, and that the perfection of virtue does not consist in losing these things and despising them. And that the latter, that is the inward things, are the better, and by losing them a grief that cannot be shaken off occurs. Therefore he boldly contradicted what God had said, and declared that Job does not deserve praise at all, since he had not been subjected to a temptation that touched him himself but touched what is outside him. For he gave his skin in place of the skin of his children, and lost only his money to secure the health of his body.

2.4.0.en: “But put forth thine hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse thee to thy face” [5].

2.4.1.en: Satan asked that God Himself stretch out His hand to strike his bone and his flesh, for the thorn in the flesh is extremely severe, hard to bear without the grace of Christ (2 Cor 12:7-9).

2.5.1.en: Behold, he is in thine hand; but preserve his soul” [6].

2.5.2.en: The phrase “but preserve his soul” can be understood to mean that the temptation has limits, namely preserving his soul, not destroying it. That is, temptation reveals man's weakness, so he humbles himself before God, and his soul is preserved from pride. But if it exceeds the limits of man's capacity, he falls into despair and frustration afflicts it, and his soul perishes because of his unbelief.

2.5.3.en: The Lord set a limit to the temptation: “but preserve his soul,” that is, do not bring him to death. Satan was eager to kill him at one of his moments of weakness after driving him to blaspheme. But God bound Satan so that he would not kill him.

2.5.4.en: Some interpret the expression “preserve his soul” as “preserve his mind,” meaning that He permitted him bodily illnesses without his losing his ability to reason and think.

2.5.5.en: St. John Chrysostom comments on this phrase to show how weak Satan is, for though he is like a ravening beast, and without a body, he cannot approach to tempt a human being who bears a body except by God's permission.

2.5.6.en: * “Preserve his soul,” meaning do not kill him. In this he has no authority over that unless he receives permission for it... We understand from this that his authority is conditional upon being permitted or refused... The expression “preserve his soul” is stronger than “do not touch his life.”

2.5.7.en: * Do not fear, then, Satan, even though he is bodiless, when he draws near to the body. For there is none weaker than that one who draws near in this manner though he is not clothed in a body, and none stronger than the brave and bold one, even if he carries a mortal body!

2.5.8.en: St. John Chrysostom * It was said to the enemy when he asked for him: “Behold, he is in thine hand.” (Job 2:6) The same person is in the hand of God and at the same time in the hand of Satan...

2.5.9.en: But how is it said to Satan: “But preserve his soul”? For how can he preserve who always longs to destroy the things preserved? Satan's preserving him here means his not daring to destroy. Just as we speak with the Father in prayer, asking: “Lead us not into temptation,” because God will not lead anyone into temptation, for He always overshadows His servants with His mercy to protect them from temptation. Yet if He does not protect us from the allurements of temptation, it is as though He leads us into temptation. Thus, by not allowing us to be tempted above what we are able, it is as though He does not lead us into the snare of temptation.

2.5.10.en: In the same way as it is said to God: “Lead us not into temptation” if He permits our adversary to lead us into it, so it is said of our adversary that he “preserves our soul” when he is bound not to overcome us by his temptation.

2.5.12.en: * Now I give you the right to turn things upside down. I deliver him to you (Job 2:6), not that you may change his spirit (his thought), nor that you may have authority over his will, nor that you may destroy his freedom in his decision, because if you used pressure on these things you would easily triumph over him, and the battle would be unfair... Surely you would like to approach the “life” of the righteous man, but you cannot, because the law of the great King avenges this, otherwise the guardian of the flock would have let the wolf loose. I deliver to you the life of those whom you envy, not to do whatever you wish, but in the fear of my laws and my divine will...

2.5.13.en: You are unable to say that another attacks Job's life, because you are the one who attacks it, you whom I appoint as its keeper. You will be condemned if you lay an ambush for his life.

2.5.14.en: * Here the protective guard goes hand in hand with permission to strike, and the divine dispensation is accomplished through the protection and through the abandonment of the chosen servant; while He abandons him, He guards him... Thus the saint was delivered into the hand of the adversary, but his soul is kept in the hand of (God) his helper, for he is among the flock of which the Truth said in the Gospel: “neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand” (Jn 10:28).

2.5.15.en: Moreover, they do not see Lucifer rise, he of whom Isaiah said: [Lucifer, who rose in the morning], then continues [he is cut down to the ground] (Isa 14:12), indicating that he does not return to regain his former dignity. By his fall from heaven to earth he wanted the destruction of man, but God gives the one who is not deceived authority to tread the traitor under his feet, and to shatter him into pieces.

2.5.16.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem *The unclean spirit has no authority over human beings. This is shown in his struggle against the blessed Job, for he took authority over his body from the Lord, who said to him: “Behold, he is in thine hand; but preserve his soul” (Job 2:6), that is, do not weaken his spirit and make him mad, and gain dominion over his memory and mind, strangling his inner strength.

2.5.17.en: Fr. Serenus * He put the saint's body into Satan's hands, but his vital powers were withheld from him. For if Satan had struck that on which his senses and his rational faculty depend, the sin arising from the misuse of the faculties would have arisen and remained at his door, not by his desire to commit it but because of the imbalance of his mind.

2.5.18.en: St. Jerome St. Ambrose offers us a wonderful interpretation of this phrase, in his discourse on St. Paul's imitation of God:

2.5.19.en: * Everyone who believes is received by the Lord, but He chastens every son whom He receives (Heb 12:6). And in His chastening of him He does not deliver him to death. For it is written: [The LORD hath chastened me sore: but he hath not given me over unto death] (Ps 118:18).

2.5.20.en: The Apostle Paul teaches us not to abandon those who have committed sin unto death, but to bind them to the bread of tears (of repentance), yet let their sorrow be moderate. This is what the phrase means: “thou givest them tears to drink in great measure” (Ps 80:5). Their sorrow must be in measure, lest the penitent be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. As he said to the Corinthians: “What will ye? shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?” (1 Cor 4:21). He uses the rod, but without harshness, for it is said: “Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell” (Prov 23:14).

2.5.21.en: And what the Apostle means by the rod appeared when he rebuked the sin of fornication (1 Cor 5:1), warning against immorality with relatives whom it is forbidden to marry, and reproving their pride, since those who ought to have mourned were puffed up. And finally, in speaking of the offender he commanded that he be removed from the congregation and delivered to Satan, not for the destruction of his soul but for the destruction of his body.

2.5.22.en: And in this Paul imitates God, who did not give Satan authority over the spirit of the blessed Job, but permitted him to afflict his body (Job 2:6). Paul delivered the sinner to Satan for the destruction of the body, so that the serpent might lick the dust of his body (Mic 7:17), but as for his spirit, it will not harm it...

2.5.23.en: And if we want to explain what the Apostle Paul means, let us consider his very words, in what sense he said to deliver him to Satan for the destruction of the body, because it is Satan who tempts us, bringing infirmities and diseases upon our bodies. Satan smote the blessed Job with bitter sores from the sole of his foot to his head, because he received authority for the destruction of his body, when the Lord said to him: “Behold, he is in thine hand; but preserve his soul” (Job 2:6). This is also what the Apostle took up in the same words, delivering the fornicator to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, “that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus” (1 Cor 5:5).

2.5.24.en: Great is this authority!! And great is this gift, by which Satan destroys himself by himself, by urging the tempting of man, for he makes him strong in spirit instead of weak. For when his body is weakened his spirit grows strong, because the weakness of the body resists sin, whereas its delicate living kindles the fire of sin.

2.5.25.en: Satan was deceived, for he wounded himself by the blows he directed against himself, fighting himself by his thought of weakening the sinner. Thus Satan armed Job the more when he wounded him. For when his whole body was worn away with sores, he truly bore Satan's blow without anything of his venom touching him, and thus it was truly said of him: [Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook?... Wilt thou play with him as with a bird? or wilt thou bind him for thy maidens?... Lay thine hand upon him] (Job 41:5).

2.5.26.en: See how Paul mocked Satan, so that he became like the child mentioned in the prophecy who put his hand on the serpent without its harming him. He drew him out of his hiding places and turned his venom into a spiritual antidote against poisons. Turning the poison into a remedy for the poison that is used for the destruction of the body, it became a cure for the spirit!

2.5.27.en: Then let me leave the serpent to strike what is earthly in (my body), let me leave it to bite my flesh and cause it to turn livid, and righteousness will say to it concerning me: “Behold, he is in thine hand; but preserve his soul” (Job 2:6).

2.5.28.en: How mighty is God!! He delivers the keeping of man's soul into the hand of Satan who wants his destruction...!! By the Master's commandments He made Satan a keeper of His sheep, so that against his will he came to carry out the commandments of heaven, and in his harshness he obeys the commandments of gentleness!

2.6.s.en: 2. Another Adam in the midst of the ashes

2.6.0.en: 7 So went Satan forth from the presence of the LORD, and smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown. 8 And he took him a potsherd to scrape himself withal; and he sat down among the ashes.

2.6.1.en: “So went Satan forth from the presence of the LORD, and smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown” [7].

2.6.2.en: As soon as Satan received permission he pounced on Job's body to strike it with an extremely violent disease. He did not strike him with a single sore, nor with several sores, but with sores from the sole of his foot, so that he was unable to walk, to his crown. He could not sleep on either side, nor on his back or even his stomach, nor sit, nor stand, for his whole body except his tongue was full of sores. He did not even find dogs to lick his sores, as happened with poor Lazarus (Lk 16:21).

2.6.3.en: Origen comments on the divine promise: [If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the LORD thy God, and wilt give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of these diseases upon thee, which I have brought upon the Egyptians] (Ex 15:26). [Since one of their diseases was boils, why did Job fall into this disease? The boils of the pagan Egyptians are their weaknesses toward the love of the world and what is in it. This is what the Lord heals us from, and does not put upon us.]

2.6.4.en: * [All things work together for good to them that love God] (Rom 8:28). Job, the holy man, was tried. He lost his sons and daughters, his house fell in ruin, and he lost all he had; suddenly everything was gone! He was no longer a father or a master, and there was no sound member left in his body except his tongue, with which he could blaspheme. Behold the tempter, for Scripture says: “smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown” (Job 2:7)...

2.6.5.en: He left him only his tongue so that he might be able to blaspheme his God. [In all this did not Job sin with his lips] (Job 1:22).

2.6.6.en: Only realize the dreadfulness of the trial. Consider the greatness of his virtue. Consider well and understand how the saying of the Apostle was fulfilled: [All things work together for good to them that love God]... Before the trial God never spoke with him; and after he was tried God came to him and spoke with him, setting aside formality, as a friend with his friend.

2.6.7.en: Let calamity strike, let every kind of calamity come, so long as Christ comes after the calamity.

2.6.8.en: St. Jerome * Perhaps because our God knows that I am exceedingly weak He did not give him authority over my body. Even though I myself desire that. For although I offer myself (to accept a trial in the body), God reckoned me unworthy of this struggle, and tested me with various troubles. But Job did not begin with this struggle; he ended with it.

2.7.0.en: St. Ambrose “And he took him a potsherd to scrape himself withal; and he sat down among the ashes” [8].

2.7.1.en: What is this potsherd (fragments of earthen vessels) with which he scratches his body afflicted with sores, if not the use of earthly or temporal means for healing the soul? Instead of offering true comforts and real healing, the person uses a potsherd which causes the sores to be even more contaminated, and wrecks the body; so when we stretch out our hands to treat our spiritual illnesses by human ways apart from God's grace, we wreck our souls all the more and destroy them.

2.7.2.en: Job became a type of the Lord Christ, for Job found no place to lay his head, and had nothing before him but to sit on a dunghill amid sores that filled his whole body, mocked even by his friends. So the Son of Man has not where to lay His head, and has nothing but to be lifted up on the Cross amid the pains of His whole body; His own received Him not (Jn 1:11).

2.7.3.en: Job did not go up on a mountain, but sat on a dunghill, to enjoy there victory over the enemy of good, glorifying God his God. So our Christ, the Savior of the world, rests in the humble and the contrite of heart to raise up a temple for Himself from them. He chose the foolish things to put to shame the wise, and the weak things to put to shame the strong, and the base things and things which are despised, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are (1 Cor 1:27-28).

2.7.4.en: Job found no one to sympathize with him, nor anyone to bandage his sores; perhaps his friends feared the enemy or could not bear the stench of the sores. He did not find a piece of cloth with which to clean his wounds, but scraped them with a potsherd, so the remedy was more painful than the disease itself. There was no one to anoint the wounds of the sores with antiseptic substances nor with ointment to soothe the pain! He complained later, saying that his flesh was clothed with worms and clods of dust (Job 7:5).

2.7.5.en: As for his sitting in the ashes with his whole body full of sores, it increased the contamination of his wounds instead of cleansing them. Perhaps he did this as a sign of his humility, contrition and repentance.

2.7.6.en: In the Septuagint it reads: “He sat upon a dunghill outside the city.”

2.7.7.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) says that we should not marvel if one whom God Himself praised is permitted to be tried until he sits in the midst of the ashes, just as St. John the Baptist, to whom He bore witness that among those born of women there is none greater than he, was permitted to have his life given as the price of a wanton dance.

2.7.8.en: * Is it not (permitted) so that He may press them down below, in order to reward them on high?

2.7.9.en: He brings them down outwardly to the level of contempt, so as to lead them inwardly to the heights that cannot be comprehended.

2.7.11.en: * Since human medicines could not heal him, patience and faith healed him. He sat on a heap of dung, but his soul was walking about in Paradise.

2.7.12.en: St. Jerome * He brought him down from the royal throne to sit on a dunghill. And though resisted by the woes I just referred to, he remained sound. His body was torn, but he kept in the depths of his soul the treasure of godliness inviolate.

2.7.13.en: St. Basil the Great * O man corrupt (in body), yet innocent! O being branded (with sores), yet beautiful! Wounded, yet your soul is full of health! You sit on a dunghill, and reign in heaven!

2.7.14.en: If we love, let us imitate him, and let us strive to follow his example.

2.7.15.en: Fr. Caesarius, bishop of Arles * Do you not see that he truly came to the utmost destitution, so that it is impossible for you to find anyone with whom to compare him? For how could there be anyone poorer than a naked man who has no roof to take shelter under? Indeed, it was not within his power to enjoy even the ground, but he sat on a dunghill.

2.7.16.en: Therefore, when you find that you have reached poverty, consider the sufferings of the righteous man, and immediately you will rise and shake off from yourselves every thought of despair.

2.7.17.en: This trial seems to men to be the foundation of all sufferings put together. But the second trial that follows it, or rather precedes it, is the sorrows of the body. Who became so disabled as he? Who bore such a disease? Who ever received or heard of anyone who fell under such great sorrows? No one.

2.7.18.en: His body wore away little by little, and a stream of worms came forth from his members on every side; this torrent overflowed without ceasing, the foul stench surrounded him powerfully, the body was destroyed bit by bit, and corruption with such putrefaction made his food bitter, and hunger became to him strange and singular.

2.7.19.en: He was not able to enjoy even the food that was offered him, for he says: [I see my food has become loathsome] (Job 6:7). When you fall under weakness, O man, remember that holy body. It was a holy and pure body even while afflicted with such wounds...

2.7.20.en: But someone may say, he had great comfort and relief, since he knew that it was God who brought these troubles upon him. This in fact makes his distress greater and more bewildering, that the righteous God whom he served in every way entered into war with him... He says: “Wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?” (Job 40:8).

2.7.21.en: When he felt guilty he said: “I will lay mine hand upon my mouth. Once have I spoken; but I will not answer: yea, twice; but I will proceed no further” (Job 40:4-5). Again he says: “I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:5-6).

2.7.22.en: But if you think there is in this sufficient comfort, you are able to experience the same comfort. And if you suffer nothing of this from the hand of God, but from the arrogance of men, then give thanks to God and do not blaspheme the One who is able to truly restrain them. And if He permitted them to do so, it is for your testing; for whoever suffers sufferings from the hand of God is crowned. So you also are crowned, because you bear with godliness the misfortunes that men brought upon you, giving thanks to the One who is able to prevent them from doing so, but did not will it.

2.7.23.en: * The wounds of the righteous man (Job) became more profitable than pearls...

2.7.24.en: Picture this wrestler before you, and imagine him in the mire, sitting in the midst of it.

2.7.25.en: What a golden statue studded with jewels!

2.7.26.en: I do not know how to express this, for I am unable to find a material so precious to compare with this body stained with blood. It is far more precious than any material, whatever its cost, for the nature of that body is incomparably precious, and those wounds are brighter than the rays of the sun, for these (the sun's rays) enlighten the eyes of the body, but those enlighten the eyes of the soul! They strike Satan with a total, unrelieved blindness.

2.7.27.en: * Do you realize, beloved, how great was the reward of the trial?

2.7.28.en: His body was agile and sound, but it became more dignified when it was pierced with wounds...!

2.7.29.en: A king sitting on the throne is not, in renown, equal to this man sitting in the mire with great standing... for after the royal throne comes death, but after the mire the Kingdom of Heaven.

2.7.30.en: * Why did he sit on a dunghill? To hide, on the heap of refuse, his fall (unto death).

2.7.31.en: Why did he go outside the gates? In order to find some relief, for if he had remained in a closed room, however pure the air of the room, it would be spoiled, and he himself would be suffocated by the foul smell.

2.7.32.en: In my opinion his sufferings had absolutely no human cause, and he understood that God wished to give a lesson by what happened to him, so he felt neither shame nor embarrassment, but showed himself as having become a laughingstock to all.

2.7.33.en: St. John Chrysostom * In any case Job did well to sit on a dunghill... for his worn-out body became refuse. He remembered that the body contains the same components (as the dunghill).

2.8.0.en: 9 Then said his wife unto him, Dost thou still retain thine integrity? Bless God, and die. 10 But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips.

2.8.2.en: Dost thou still retain thine integrity?

2.8.3.en: Bless God, and die (blaspheme against God, and die!)” [9].

2.8.4.en: The Septuagint reads: “And when a long time had passed, his wife said to him: How long will you endure, saying: Behold, I wait a little longer, expecting the hope of my salvation?” [9 (a)]

2.8.5.en: It is also found in the Septuagint that Job's wife used to wander from house to house, hoping to find a refuge in which to take shelter.

2.8.6.en: Some of the Jews consider that Job's wife is Dinah the daughter of Jacob.

2.8.7.en: The enemy is accustomed to strike the faithful through the members of their own household, as he did with Adam using Eve, and with David using his wife Michal, who mocked David her husband, and he even wanted to use the Apostle Peter to strike the Lord Christ when He spoke of the Crucifixion, so that he said to Him: “Be it far from thee, Lord: this shall not be unto thee” (Mt 16:22). So He turned and said to Peter: “Get thee behind me, Satan: thou art an offence unto me: for thou savourest not the things that be of God, but those that be of men” (Mt 16:23).

2.8.8.en: The righteous Job expressed his wife's view of him, saying: “My breath is loathsome to my wife, and I have become foul (a stench) to the children of my body” (Job 19:17).

2.8.9.en: * Satan left him nothing but his tongue and his wife. Through his wife he tempts him, and with his tongue he can blaspheme. Satan did not forget his old deception by which he deceived Adam through a woman, therefore he attacked Job through his wife, reckoning that he would always be able to deceive him by a woman, not realizing that if one man was mortally wounded by a woman, now the whole world has been saved through a woman.

2.8.11.en: The first drove us out of Paradise, and the last led us (by Christ her Son) to heaven.

2.8.12.en: St. Jerome * [And when a long time was passed] [Job 2:9] LXX... The Spirit kept the expressions quite plain for our benefit, as He did not declare the length of this period. For had He specified months and years, those who are placed under trial in the future would be disheartened before reaching the end of the period. They would count the nights and the hours, and focus on this time. Each of them would fall into extreme despair that God's hand had not intervened, and that he had not received help from the heavens as Job did at a set time.

2.8.13.en: In fact the Spirit said: “a long time.” He expressed it thus in order that you may know that Job was found stronger, not only than the illness and the many sores, but also than time.

2.8.14.en: He wrestled for a long time in bodily torments and troubles, and yet he remained unconquered in the battles.

2.8.15.en: By this the Spirit comforts us that however long the time of trial, our heart should not grow weak, for God's hand will come and His right hand will be for our sake (Ps 18:35), for Job was saved from the furnace of trial after a long time.

2.8.16.en: * Since the adversary did not find the fighter weakened, he enlisted his wife. Perhaps he said to himself: This person (Job) will not be stronger than Adam. If he is rich, yet he does not have “the Paradise of God” (like Adam in the garden). And although righteous, he has not attained “the tree of life.” And although godly, Adam enjoyed conversation with God. This person (Job) has many cattle, but as for Adam, all the beasts of the earth were subject to him. Therefore if I was able to make him lose this through Eve his wife, perhaps this one cannot resist the assaults of his wife. With this thought Satan stirred up Job's wife against him.

2.8.17.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * He left his wife to him alone, not as a comforter but rather as Satan's ally.

2.8.18.en: St. Augustine The continuation of the verse in the Septuagint reads: “Behold, your memory has been blotted out from the earth, even your sons and daughters, the pangs of my travail and the toils of my womb, whom I bore with sorrows in vain; and behold, you sit spending your nights in the open air amid the corruption of worms, and I have become a wanderer and a servant, moving from place to place and from house to house, awaiting the setting of the sun that I may rest from my labors and pains which have encompassed me. Say some word against God, and die” [Job 2:9 - LXX].

2.8.19.en: * Imagine that you have lost your wealth through which you were famous. The same if you have been deprived of your share in sons; how can your memory remain on the earth after that time? Your goods have been stolen, your possessions destroyed, there are no more sons, no daughters remain, and there will be no children (grandchildren), since the sons have been lost.

2.8.20.en: (As though Job's wife were saying to her husband): In vain have I sown the field of my womb.

2.8.21.en: You yourself have been deprived of what you planted, and I too have lost the fruit of my sorrows and the toil of my breasts, and the experience of the womb of pregnant women, the unbearable pangs of labor, which are reckoned as a dreadful memory.

2.8.22.en: Then is it one sorrow or many sorrows...?

2.8.23.en: Death has reached the children of my womb, and the fruit of my body has perished in the abyss.

2.8.24.en: Can I hope to conceive other children?

2.8.25.en: How? Where? For the sower, who is you, has been ruined and has perished, and you yourself have become food for vermin.

2.8.26.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * The more the calamities he brought upon him increased, the more he saw him in strength. Therefore, as you know, after he had used every means, finally he used his instrument; for when he found no way for himself, he ran to his old weapon, the woman, and put on the mask of concern, and presented a tragic picture of his disasters in a tone of the utmost tenderness, and under the pretense of removing his evil offered fatal counsel (curse the Lord and die). But not even by this did he conquer, indeed because that wonderful man recognized his deceit, and with great wisdom silenced the woman who was speaking at his instigation.

2.8.27.en: * See how she tried by her eloquence to reach all the way to the end. For she has a multitude of arguments with which to persuade him.

2.8.28.en: As for the length of time, since not one day passed, nor two nor three days, but a great number of months. How long will you endure...?

2.8.29.en: Note the satanic deception, for he thought of Eve. He says: Behold, you who caused the first man to fall can end the life of Job.

2.8.30.en: But she was foolish and poor, for finding Adam unable to overcome his weakness, she was able to put poison in good food.

2.8.31.en: Behold, you see that Job, on the contrary, was a wise man, victorious even over his nature... So do not think that the matter concerns the woman or her recommendations...

2.8.32.en: Now I suggest to our people that they not take into account the dignity of persons, but rather the nature of the counsel.

2.8.33.en: For the woman came to help the man, not to be a stumbling block to him... He expects a change, something indicating sound faith and noble hope; he knows God's tenderness.

2.8.34.en: Thus the main lines of the foundation of her wickedness were laid down. She did not say: “They have died,” according to the common expression used to indicate general grief among all men, for she did not use the usual expression. But what did she say? [Your memory has been blotted out...]

2.8.35.en: In my opinion she wished to justify the violence of the trial by speaking thus.

2.8.36.en: This is what she wanted to say to him: “What kind of change do you hope will occur? Can you return to what you were after all that has happened, for can what has utterly vanished return to life?

2.8.37.en: For we desire children, often so that they may extend our memory in a way that does not pass away. Surely the most important thing men seek is to leave memorials after them. She says to him: You yourself are dead by the loss of your children, for without offspring and without children you perish.

2.8.38.en: Note to what level she offered this terrible counsel, not to urge him to anger, but to turn him aside to self-pity...

2.8.39.en: She says: Night and day you find no one to share the roof of your house with you, no one to console you, no one to pity you, no one to share your pains...

2.8.40.en: What wretchedness! There is no one to pity his wife, nor to soothe her circumstances, she who was in the company of a king has become a slave living in the open under the stars...” For I am without a house or a city or a home, I go about in the city... there is not one house to lighten the shame of my condition, and everywhere I receive mockery and insult from the common people”.

2.8.41.en: She did not say to him: “Blaspheme,” but said: [Curse God...] Why? So that you may know that by doing this you die, but as for my death, what consolation could it bring you? What correction of the situation by my death...?

2.8.42.en: What are you saying, woman? When it is necessary to beseech God to grant good things, when it is necessary to appease Him, you are ready to provoke Him! If God is the source of these troubles, then it calls for supplication to Him, not blasphemy against Him. And on the other hand, if He is not their source, then He is not to be blasphemed!

2.8.43.en: St. John Chrysostom * Job lost his children and all he owned except his wife! (Job 1:13-19), who alone was preserved for his temptation! (Job 2:9-10). And at that time he was covered all over with deadly sores (Job 2:7), and he realized that his friends had not come to console him, but to increase his sufferings and magnify them!

2.8.44.en: Note the authority that was given to the adversary by the Lord to try him (Job 2:1-6). And although he felt that the arrows of the Lord were in his flesh, and said that they had pierced his body (Job 6:4), yet as a good wrestler he did not yield to the pain, nor refuse the difficulties of the struggle, but continued.

2.8.45.en: “Since the Lord has begun, let Him wound me, but do not stab me (destroy me) in the end, for what is my strength that I should be silent (wait)?

2.8.46.en: And what is my end that my soul should endure?

2.8.47.en: Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh of brass?

2.8.48.en: Have I not trust in Him? But help has forsaken me, and His visitation has despised me” (Job 6:9, 11-14) LXX.

2.8.49.en: St. Ambrose * In truth his wife alone had been left until that day. All that he had was completely destroyed, all his children and possessions and even his body, and she was left for the temptation to be a snare for him.

2.8.50.en: This is truly the reason why Satan did not destroy her along with the children, and did not ask for her death, since he expected that she would contribute the more to making the holy man fall into the snare. Therefore he left her as a kind of terrible instrument in his hand.

2.8.51.en: He said: “If even in Paradise humanity was driven out by her means, how much more can I cast him down while he is on the dunghill!”

2.8.52.en: * The building was the same (the one on the rock and the one on the sand), and the trials were the same, but the end was not the same, because the foundation was different. The fall of the building occurred because of the foolishness of the builder and not because of the nature of the trials,...

2.8.53.en: Do not think that these things were said about a mere building, but the discourse concerns the soul, affirming that by its works it hears the divine Word or rejects it. Thus Job built himself.

2.8.54.en: The rain came down, because fire came down from heaven and consumed all his flocks, and the floods came, as the messengers came to him bearing news of disasters in continuous succession, telling him of the destruction of his flocks, his camels and his sons. And the wind blew, which is the bitter words of his wife, saying: [Curse God and die]. Yet the house did not fall. His soul was not moved from its place, and the righteous man did not blaspheme, but gave thanks to God, saying: [The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; what is good in His eyes He does].
